module.title: Unit 11: Animal World: Past Simple Regular Verbs
module.objective: Use the Past Simple with regular verbs to recount past events, and ask and answer questions about past activities.

subModules.title: Reading Mission: Animals in the Past
subModules.grammarFocus: Past Simple Regular Verbs (affirmative, negative, and question forms)
subModules.vocabularyFocus: Animals, animal actions, past time expressions, and regular verb forms

content.summary: Welcome to your Reading Mission about the Animal World! In this lesson, you will read a fun story about animals and what happened to them in the past. You will learn to understand Past Simple regular verbs — words that end in -ed — to talk about things that already happened. By the end of this mission, you will feel confident reading short stories about animals and their past adventures. Let's explore the animal world together!

linguisticTarget.grammar: Past Simple regular verbs: affirmative (walked, played, helped), negative (didn't walk, didn't play), and question forms (Did you walk? Did she play?). Spelling rules for adding -ed.
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Animal names (dog, cat, parrot, rabbit, turtle, elephant), animal actions (walked, played, jumped, cleaned, carried, followed), and past time expressions (yesterday, last week, last year, two days ago).
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Skimming the passage first to understand the main idea, then scanning for specific details such as animal names, actions in the past, and time expressions. Look for words ending in -ed to identify past actions.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a short A1 passage about animals and their past activities.
Identify key details including which animals did what, when events happened, and how people helped animals.
Recognize Past Simple regular verbs (words ending in -ed) and understand their meaning in context.
Distinguish between affirmative, negative, and question forms of Past Simple regular verbs in a reading passage.
Use time expressions (yesterday, last week, last year) to understand when past events happened.

contextWarmup.prompt: Read this sentence: 'The dog played in the park yesterday.' What does 'played' tell us?
options: The dog did this action in the past — it is finished.
The dog is playing right now.
contextWarmup.explanation: Great job! The word 'played' ends in -ed. This tells us the action happened in the past and is already finished. The word 'yesterday' also helps us know it was in the past.

rules: When you see a verb ending in -ed in a sentence, it usually means the action happened in the past. For example: 'The cat jumped on the table.' (The jumping already happened.)
In negative sentences, look for 'didn't' + base verb (no -ed). For example: 'The dog didn't play outside.' The word 'didn't' already shows the past, so 'play' stays in its base form.
In questions, look for 'Did' at the beginning + base verb (no -ed). For example: 'Did the parrot talk?' The word 'Did' already shows the past.
Time expressions like 'yesterday,' 'last week,' 'last month,' 'two days ago,' and 'last year' are clues that the sentence is about the past.

Spelling tip: If a verb ends in -e, just add -d (love → loved). If a verb ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed (carry → carried). If a short verb ends in consonant-vowel-consonant, double the last letter and add -ed (stop → stopped).

commonTrap.explanation: Many beginners add -ed to the verb even after 'didn't' or 'Did.' Remember: 'didn't' and 'Did' already show the past tense, so the main verb must stay in its base form (without -ed).
commonTrap.wrong: Did the cat jumped on the table? / The dog didn't walked home.
commonTrap.correct: Did the cat jump on the table? / The dog didn't walk home.

sections.title: Reading Passage: A Special Day at the Animal Shelter

content.passageTitle: A Special Day at the Animal Shelter
content.context: Maria and her brother Leo visited an animal shelter last Saturday. Read about their day and the animals they met.
content.text:
Last Saturday, Maria and her brother Leo visited an animal shelter near their house. They wanted to help the animals there.

First, Maria cleaned the cages for the rabbits. The rabbits jumped and played happily. Leo walked two big dogs in the park. The dogs loved it! One brown dog followed Leo everywhere.

After that, they helped the workers. They carried food and water to the birds. A green parrot talked and repeated funny words. Maria laughed a lot!

At the end of the day, Maria and Leo talked to the shelter manager. 'Did you enjoy your day?' the manager asked. 'Yes, we loved it!' Maria answered.

The family decided to adopt a small white cat. They named her Snowball. Maria and Leo were very happy. They walked home with Snowball in a special box. It was a wonderful day!

highlights.note: Past Simple of 'visit' — add -ed to the base verb.
Past Simple of 'carry' — change y to i, then add -ed.
A place where animals without homes can live safely.
Past Simple of 'adopt' — to take an animal home as a pet.
Past Simple question form: Did + subject + base verb (no -ed).
A time expression that tells us this happened in the past.

gistQuestion.prompt: What is the main idea of the passage?
options: Maria and Leo visited an animal shelter, helped the animals, and adopted a cat.
Maria and Leo went to school and studied about animals.
Maria and Leo watched a movie about animals at home.
gistQuestion.explanation: The passage tells us about Maria and Leo's visit to an animal shelter. They helped the animals by cleaning cages, walking dogs, and carrying food. At the end, they adopted a small white cat named Snowball.

detailQuestions.prompt: What did Maria do first at the shelter?
options: She cleaned the cages for the rabbits.
She walked two big dogs in the park.
She carried food to the birds.
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'First, Maria cleaned the cages for the rabbits.' The word 'First' tells us this was her first activity at the shelter.

detailQuestions.prompt: What did the brown dog do?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'One brown dog followed Leo everywhere.' The Past Simple verb 'followed' tells us this action happened during their visit.

detailQuestions.prompt: What animal did the family adopt?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'The family decided to adopt a small white cat. They named her Snowball.' So the correct answer is a small white cat.

detailQuestions.prompt: What question did the shelter manager ask?
detailQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'Did you enjoy your day?' the manager asked. Notice the Past Simple question form: Did + subject + base verb (enjoy, not enjoyed).

questions.question: According to the passage, when did Maria and Leo visit the animal shelter?
questions.explanation: The very first sentence says: 'Last Saturday, Maria and Leo visited an animal shelter near their house.' The time expression 'Last Saturday' tells us exactly when the visit happened.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the correct Past Simple negative form?
options: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
Maria didn't cleaned the dog cages.
Maria not cleaned the dog cages.
questions.answer: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
questions.explanation: In Past Simple negative sentences, we use 'didn't' + base verb (without -ed). 'Didn't clean' is correct. 'Didn't cleaned' is wrong because we don't add -ed after 'didn't.'

questions.question: In the passage, what did the green parrot do?
options: It talked and repeated funny words.
It jumped out of the cage.
questions.answer: It talked and repeated funny words.
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'A green parrot talked and repeated funny words.' Both 'talked' and 'repeated' are Past Simple regular verbs ending in -ed.

questions.question: What is the correct Past Simple form of the verb 'carry'?
questions.explanation: When a verb ends in consonant + y (like 'carry'), we change the y to i and add -ed. So 'carry' becomes 'carried.' This spelling rule is important to remember!

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'They walked home with Snowball in a special box.' What does 'walked' tell us?
options: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
questions.answer: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
questions.explanation: The verb 'walked' ends in -ed, which means it is in the Past Simple tense. This tells us the action already happened and is complete. The whole story is about events that happened last Saturday.

questions.question: Which is the correct Past Simple question form?
questions.explanation: In Past Simple questions, we use 'Did' + subject + base verb (without -ed). 'Did they help' is correct. We don't add -ed to the verb after 'Did' because 'Did' already shows the past tense.

questions.question: What name did Maria and Leo give to their new cat?
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'They named her Snowball.' The verb 'named' is also a Past Simple regular verb (name → named: just add -d because the base verb already ends in -e).

questions.question: Look at these two sentences: 'Leo walked two big dogs.' and 'Leo didn't walk the cats.' Why does the second sentence use 'walk' instead of 'walked'?
options: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
Because negative sentences are always in the present tense.
questions.answer: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
questions.explanation: This is a very important rule! In negative Past Simple sentences, 'didn't' carries the past meaning. The main verb returns to its base form (walk, not walked). This is a common mistake for beginners, so remember: didn't + base verb.

subModules.title: Listening Mission: Animals We Loved and Helped

content.summary: In this listening mission, you will hear a conversation between two friends talking about their experiences with animals in the past. They use Past Simple regular verbs like 'walked', 'played', 'cleaned', and 'watched'. Pay close attention to the '-ed' ending on verbs. Sometimes '-ed' sounds like /t/ (walked), sometimes like /d/ (played), and sometimes like /ɪd/ (wanted). Listen for time words like 'yesterday', 'last week', and 'last summer' to know the speakers are talking about the past.
learningObjectives: Identify Past Simple regular verbs with '-ed' endings when spoken in natural conversation.
Understand questions and answers about past activities with animals.
Recognise time expressions such as 'yesterday', 'last week', and 'last summer' in spoken English.
Distinguish between the three pronunciations of '-ed': /t/, /d/, and /ɪd/.

keyPhrases.note: Use 'walked' (Past Simple of 'walk') with a time word like 'yesterday' to talk about a finished action.

keyPhrases.phrase: We cleaned the cage last week.
keyPhrases.note: 'Cleaned' ends with a /d/ sound. 'Last week' tells us when it happened.
'Played' is a regular Past Simple verb. The '-ed' sounds like /d/ after a vowel sound.

keyPhrases.phrase: Did you visit the animal shelter?
keyPhrases.meaning: Apakah kamu mengunjungi tempat penampungan hewan?
keyPhrases.note: Use 'Did you + base verb' to ask about the past. Do not add '-ed' after 'did'.
'Wanted' has the /ɪd/ sound because the base verb 'want' ends in a 't' sound.

keyPhrases.phrase: They watched the birds in the park.
keyPhrases.note: 'Watched' ends with a /t/ sound because the base verb 'watch' ends in a /tʃ/ sound.

connectedSpeech.note: The '-ed' in 'walked' is pronounced as a quick /t/ sound. It does not add an extra syllable. Listen carefully because it can be very short in fast speech.
The '-ed' in 'cleaned' sounds like /d/. In fast speech, 'we' shortens slightly and the /d/ blends into 'the'.
'Did you' often blends together in natural speech to sound like 'didju'. The /d/ and /j/ merge into a /dʒ/ sound.
'Wanted' has two syllables: 'want-id'. The /ɪd/ ending is used because the base verb ends in a /t/ sound. In fast speech the second /t/ may soften.
The '-ed' in 'played' is a /d/ sound that blends smoothly after the vowel. 'With the' can sound like 'wiv-the' in fast speech.

sections.title: Audio Dialogue: A Day at the Animal Shelter

content.context: Jenny and Pedro are talking on the phone the day after Jenny visited an animal shelter. Pedro stayed home but is curious about what Jenny did there. They talk about the animals Jenny helped and what happened during her visit.
content.audioPrompt: Listen carefully to the following dialogue between Jenny and Pedro. Pay attention to the Past Simple regular verbs they use.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.text: Hey, Jenny! How was the animal shelter yesterday?
lines.translation: Hei, Jenny! Bagaimana tempat penampungan hewan kemarin?

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: It was amazing! I walked three dogs in the morning.
lines.translation: Luar biasa! Aku mengajak tiga anjing jalan-jalan di pagi hari.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.text: Three dogs? That sounds fun! Did you play with them too?
lines.translation: Tiga anjing? Kedengarannya menyenangkan! Apakah kamu bermain dengan mereka juga?

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: Yes, I played with them in the garden. They loved it!
lines.translation: Ya, aku bermain dengan mereka di taman. Mereka suka sekali!

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.text: What about the cats? Did you help with the cats?
lines.translation: Bagaimana dengan kucingnya? Apakah kamu membantu dengan kucingnya?

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: Yes! I cleaned two cat cages and I watched the baby kittens. They were so small!
lines.translation: Ya! Aku membersihkan dua kandang kucing dan aku mengamati anak-anak kucing. Mereka sangat kecil!

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.text: Wow! Did you want to take one home?
lines.translation: Wah! Apakah kamu ingin membawa satu pulang?

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: I wanted a little orange kitten, but my mum said no. She called me and asked me to come home.
lines.translation: Aku ingin anak kucing oranye kecil, tapi ibuku bilang tidak. Dia meneleponku dan memintaku pulang.

lines.speaker: Pedro
lines.text: Oh, that is too bad. I visited my grandma last weekend. She has a pet rabbit. I helped her and I carried the rabbit food.
lines.translation: Oh, sayang sekali. Aku mengunjungi nenekku akhir pekan lalu. Dia punya kelinci peliharaan. Aku membantunya dan aku membawa makanan kelinci.

lines.speaker: Jenny
lines.text: That is nice! I really enjoyed my day at the shelter. I want to volunteer again next Saturday!
lines.translation: Itu bagus! Aku sangat menikmati hariku di penampungan. Aku ingin menjadi sukarelawan lagi Sabtu depan!

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Animal World Stories in the Past

content.summary: In this lesson, you will learn how to write sentences and short paragraphs about animals in the past. You will use Past Simple regular verbs to tell stories about what animals did yesterday, last week, or a long time ago. You will practice positive sentences (The dog played.), negative sentences (The cat didn't jump.), and questions (Did the bird fly?). Let's start writing about the animal world!

blueprintItems.title: Write a Positive Past Simple Sentence
blueprintItems.example: The elephant walked to the river yesterday.

blueprintItems.title: Write a Negative Past Simple Sentence
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + didn't + base verb + rest of sentence.
blueprintItems.example: The monkey didn't climb the tall tree.

blueprintItems.title: Write a Past Simple Question
blueprintItems.formula: Did + subject + base verb + rest of sentence?
blueprintItems.example: Did the parrot talk to you last night?

blueprintItems.title: Add Time Words to Your Story
blueprintItems.formula: Sentence + time word (yesterday / last week / two days ago).
blueprintItems.example: The rabbits hopped around the garden last Sunday.

mechanicsRules.rule: Always start a sentence with a capital letter and end with a period (.), question mark (?), or exclamation mark (!).
mechanicsRules.badExample: the cat played with a ball
mechanicsRules.goodExample: The cat played with a ball.
mechanicsRules.why: Every English sentence needs a capital letter at the start and punctuation at the end. This helps the reader know where a sentence begins and ends.

mechanicsRules.rule: In negative Past Simple sentences, use 'didn't' + the base verb. Do NOT add -ed to the verb after 'didn't'.
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'didn't' already shows the past. So the main verb stays in its base form. Adding -ed after 'didn't' is a common mistake.

mechanicsRules.rule: In Past Simple questions with 'Did', use the base verb. Do NOT add -ed to the verb after 'Did'.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Did the dog barked at the cat?
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Did the dog bark at the cat?
mechanicsRules.why: The word 'Did' at the start already shows the past tense. The main verb must stay in its base form.

mechanicsRules.rule: When adding -ed, follow the spelling rules: if the verb ends in -e, just add -d (live → lived). If it ends in consonant + y, change y to i and add -ed (carry → carried). If it ends in a short vowel + consonant, double the last consonant (stop → stopped).
mechanicsRules.why: English has special spelling rules for adding -ed. Learning these rules helps you spell past tense verbs correctly.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Animal World – Talking About the Past

content.summary: In this unit you will practise speaking about past events using Past Simple regular verbs. Regular verbs add '-ed' to the base form, but the '-ed' ending can sound three different ways: /t/, /d/, or /ɪd/. You will also practise asking and answering questions about yesterday's activities. Pay attention to how you pronounce the '-ed' ending, because it changes the rhythm and clarity of your sentences.
content.audioGuidance: Listen carefully to the '-ed' endings. After voiceless sounds like /k/, /p/, /s/, /ʃ/, /tʃ/, the '-ed' sounds like /t/ (e.g., 'walked' = /wɔːkt/). After voiced sounds like /b/, /g/, /v/, /z/, /l/, /n/, the '-ed' sounds like /d/ (e.g., 'played' = /pleɪd/). After /t/ or /d/, the '-ed' sounds like /ɪd/ and adds an extra syllable (e.g., 'visited' = /ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd/). Use falling intonation for statements about the past and rising intonation for yes/no questions like 'Did you play?'

pillars.name: The Three Sounds of '-ed'
pillars.target: Correct pronunciation of regular past tense endings
pillars.explanation: When you say 'walked', the '-ed' sounds like /t/. When you say 'played', the '-ed' sounds like /d/. When you say 'visited', the '-ed' sounds like /ɪd/ and you add one more syllable. Practise each group separately, then mix them together.

pillars.name: Past Simple Question Intonation
pillars.target: Rising intonation for yes/no questions with 'Did you…?'
pillars.explanation: When you ask 'Did you watch TV?', your voice should go UP at the end. When you answer 'Yes, I watched TV', your voice should go DOWN at the end. This pattern helps your listener know if you are asking or telling.

pillars.name: Rhythm and Stress in Past Sentences
pillars.target: Natural sentence stress when telling a story about the past
pillars.explanation: In a sentence like 'I visited my friend yesterday', the stressed words are 'VIS-it-ed', 'FRIEND', and 'YES-ter-day'. The small words like 'I' and 'my' are said quickly and softly. This gives English its natural rhythm.

pillars.name: Fluency in Storytelling
pillars.target: Speaking in connected sentences about past events
pillars.explanation: When you tell a story about yesterday, connect your sentences with words like 'and', 'then', 'after that'. For example: 'I cleaned my room and then I played with my cat.' Pause briefly between ideas, not between every word.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: 'Walked' is one syllable with the '-ed' sounding like /t/. 'Visited' has three syllables because the base verb ends in /t/, so '-ed' becomes /ɪd/. The stress stays on the first syllable: VIS-it-ed.

'Played' is one syllable with the '-ed' sounding like /d/. 'Wanted' has two syllables because the base verb ends in /t/, so '-ed' adds an extra syllable /ɪd/. Stress is on the first syllable: WANT-ed.
'Helped' is one syllable with '-ed' sounding like /t/. 'Arrived' has two syllables with stress on the second syllable: ar-RIVED. The '-ed' sounds like /d/ because /v/ is a voiced sound.
'Cleaned' is one syllable with '-ed' sounding like /d/. 'Needed' has two syllables because the base verb ends in /d/, so '-ed' adds /ɪd/. Stress is on the first syllable: NEED-ed.

drills.hint: Say 'walkt' — do not add an extra syllable. The '-ed' is silent as a separate sound; it just adds a /t/ to the end.

drills.targetText: She played with her dog in the park.
drills.phonetic: /ʃiː pleɪd wɪð hɜːr dɒɡ ɪn ðə pɑːrk/
drills.hint: Say 'playd' — the '-ed' sounds like /d/ because the vowel sound before it is voiced. Keep it one syllable.

drills.targetText: We visited the animal shelter last weekend.
drills.phonetic: /wiː ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məl ˈʃɛl.tər lɑːst ˌwiːkˈɛnd/
drills.focus: Pronouncing '-ed' as /ɪd/ after /t/ — adding an extra syllable
drills.hint: Say 'VIS-it-id' with three syllables. Because 'visit' ends in /t/, you must say the '-ed' as a separate syllable /ɪd/.

drills.targetText: Did you help your mother yesterday?
drills.focus: Rising intonation for yes/no past simple questions
drills.hint: Start the question at a normal pitch and let your voice rise on 'yesterday?' to show it is a question.

drills.targetText: I cleaned my room and then I watched TV.
drills.phonetic: /aɪ kliːnd maɪ ruːm ənd ðɛn aɪ wɒtʃt ˌtiːˈviː/
drills.focus: Connecting two past simple sentences with 'and then'
drills.hint: Say 'cleend' (one syllable, /d/ ending) and 'wotcht' (one syllable, /t/ ending). Pause briefly after 'room' before saying 'and then'.

drills.targetText: The cat jumped over the fence and landed safely.
drills.phonetic: /ðə kæt dʒʌmpt ˈəʊ.vər ðə fɛns ənd ˈlæn.dɪd ˈseɪf.li/
drills.focus: Mixing /t/ and /ɪd/ endings in one sentence
drills.hint: 'Jumped' ends in /t/ (one syllable). 'Landed' ends in /ɪd/ (two syllables: LAND-ed). Feel the difference in rhythm.

roleplay.context: You are talking with Mr. Khoirul about what you did yesterday. He asks you about your morning, afternoon, and evening activities. Use Past Simple regular verbs to describe your day. Try to use correct '-ed' pronunciation.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Hello! How are you today? Let's talk about yesterday. Where were you yesterday morning?
turns.translation: Halo! Apa kabar hari ini? Ayo kita bicara tentang kemarin. Di mana kamu kemarin pagi?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I was at home yesterday morning.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That's nice. What did you do at home? Did you watch TV or help your family?
turns.translation: Bagus. Apa yang kamu lakukan di rumah? Apakah kamu menonton TV atau membantu keluargamu?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I helped my mother in the kitchen and I watched TV after that.
turns.translation: Saya membantu ibu saya di dapur dan saya menonton TV setelah itu.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Great! And what about the afternoon? Were you at home or did you go somewhere?
turns.translation: Bagus! Dan bagaimana dengan sore harinya? Apakah kamu di rumah atau pergi ke suatu tempat?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I visited my friend's house in the afternoon. We played games together.
turns.translation: Saya mengunjungi rumah teman saya di sore hari. Kami bermain game bersama.

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Wonderful! It sounds like you had a nice day. What time did you arrive back home?
turns.translation: Luar biasa! Sepertinya kamu punya hari yang menyenangkan. Jam berapa kamu sampai di rumah?

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: I arrived home at six o'clock in the evening.
turns.translation: Saya sampai di rumah jam enam sore.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about an animal you liked when you were young. Use Past Simple regular verbs. Follow the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me a story about an animal you liked when you were a child. What animal was it? What did you do with it? What happened one special day?
storyPoints: Name the animal and describe what it looked like (e.g., 'I liked a small brown cat.')
Tell what you usually did with the animal (e.g., 'I played with it every day. I cleaned its bowl.')
Describe one special thing that happened (e.g., 'One day, it jumped on my bed and I laughed.')
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: When I was young, I liked a small cat. I played with it every day and I cleaned its bowl. One day, it jumped on my bed and I laughed.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɛn aɪ wɒz jʌŋ aɪ laɪkt ə smɔːl kæt aɪ pleɪd wɪð ɪt ˈɛv.ri deɪ ənd aɪ kliːnd ɪts bəʊl wʌn deɪ ɪt dʒʌmpt ɒn maɪ bɛd ənd aɪ lɑːft/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember: 'liked' ends in /t/, 'played' ends in /d/, 'cleaned' ends in /d/, 'jumped' ends in /t/. Keep your story simple and use past tense.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises storytelling fluency using Past Simple regular verbs. You need to connect ideas in order: introduce the animal, describe regular activities, and tell about a special event. Focus on correct '-ed' pronunciation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about a visit to a zoo or a farm. Use Past Simple regular verbs. Follow the three story points below. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please tell me about a time you visited a zoo or a farm. Where did you go? What animals did you see? What did you enjoy the most?
storyPoints: Say where you went and when (e.g., 'Last year, I visited a zoo with my family.')
Describe the animals you watched or liked (e.g., 'I watched the monkeys. They climbed the trees.')
Tell what you enjoyed the most (e.g., 'I really enjoyed the bird show. The birds danced and we clapped.')
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Last year, I visited a zoo with my family. I watched the monkeys and they climbed the trees. I really enjoyed the bird show. We clapped and laughed.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /lɑːst jɪər aɪ ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ə zuː wɪð maɪ ˈfæm.ɪ.li aɪ wɒtʃt ðə ˈmʌŋ.kiz ənd ðeɪ klaɪmd ðə triːz aɪ ˈrɪə.li ɪnˈdʒɔɪd ðə bɜːd ʃəʊ wiː klæpt ənd lɑːft/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Visited' has three syllables: VIS-it-ed (/ɪd/ ending). 'Watched' has one syllable: /wɒtʃt/ (/t/ ending). 'Enjoyed' has two syllables: en-JOYED (/d/ ending).
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task builds your ability to narrate a past experience in sequence. You practise mixing different '-ed' pronunciations in a natural story about animals.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a phone call with Mr. Khoirul. He is a zookeeper. He will ask you about your pet. Answer his questions using Past Simple regular verbs. Be ready to ask him one question too.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul from the city zoo. I heard you have a pet at home. Can you tell me about your pet? What did you do with your pet yesterday?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling the city zoo to ask about animal care. The zookeeper, Mr. Khoirul, is friendly and wants to know about your pet too. You talk about what you did with your pet yesterday and ask him about the zoo animals.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student who has a pet at home. You called the zoo because you want to learn how to take care of your pet better. Tell Mr. Khoirul what you did with your pet yesterday.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yesterday, I walked my dog in the park. I cleaned his bowl and I played with him. Did you feed the animals at the zoo today?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ aɪ wɔːkt maɪ dɒɡ ɪn ðə pɑːrk aɪ kliːnd hɪz bəʊl ənd aɪ pleɪd wɪð hɪm dɪd juː fiːd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məlz ət ðə zuː təˈdeɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use past tense for yesterday's actions: 'walked', 'cleaned', 'played'. Ask a question with 'Did you…?' and let your voice rise at the end.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises real conversation skills. You answer questions about past activities and also ask a question, showing you can use Past Simple in both statements and questions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a video call with Mr. Khoirul. He is your neighbour. His cat is missing. He asks you if you noticed anything yesterday. Answer using Past Simple regular verbs.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! This is Mr. Khoirul, your neighbour. My cat Milo is missing! I'm very worried. Did you see anything unusual yesterday near your house?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your neighbour Mr. Khoirul has lost his cat named Milo. He calls you to ask if you noticed anything yesterday. You try to help by telling him what you observed near your house yesterday.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a helpful neighbour. Yesterday you noticed a small cat near your garden. Tell Mr. Khoirul what you saw and what happened.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, I noticed a small cat near my garden yesterday. It looked scared. I tried to call it but it walked away. I searched around the garden but I didn't find it.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jɛs aɪ ˈnəʊ.tɪst ə smɔːl kæt nɪər maɪ ˈɡɑːr.dən ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ɪt lʊkt skɛəd aɪ traɪd tə kɔːl ɪt bʌt ɪt wɔːkt əˈweɪ aɪ sɜːtʃt əˈraʊnd ðə ˈɡɑːr.dən bʌt aɪ ˈdɪd.ənt faɪnd ɪt/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Noticed' = NO-ticed (two syllables, /t/ ending). 'Looked' = one syllable (/t/ ending). 'Tried' = one syllable (/d/ ending). 'Searched' = one syllable (/t/ ending).
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay builds your ability to describe past observations. You practise multiple regular past tense verbs in a realistic, helpful conversation about a missing pet.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a phone call with Mr. Khoirul. He is a veterinarian (animal doctor). You are calling because your rabbit was sick yesterday. Tell him what happened using Past Simple regular verbs.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning! This is Dr. Khoirul at the animal clinic. How can I help you today? You said your rabbit was not feeling well yesterday. Can you tell me what happened?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling the animal clinic because your pet rabbit was sick yesterday. Dr. Khoirul, the veterinarian, needs to know what symptoms you noticed and what you did to help your rabbit.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a pet owner who is worried about your rabbit. Yesterday your rabbit looked tired and didn't eat. Tell the doctor what you noticed and what you did.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yesterday, my rabbit looked very tired. It didn't move much. I offered it some food but it refused to eat. I cleaned its cage and I placed fresh water inside.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ maɪ ˈræb.ɪt lʊkt ˈvɛr.i ˈtaɪəd ɪt ˈdɪd.ənt muːv mʌtʃ aɪ ˈɒf.əd ɪt sʌm fuːd bʌt ɪt rɪˈfjuːzd tə iːt aɪ kliːnd ɪts keɪdʒ ənd aɪ pleɪst frɛʃ ˈwɔː.tər ɪnˈsaɪd/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Offered' = OF-fered (two syllables, /d/ ending). 'Refused' = re-FUSED (two syllables, /d/ ending). 'Placed' = one syllable (/t/ ending).
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises describing a problem in the past. You use Past Simple to explain symptoms and actions, which is a practical life skill when visiting an animal doctor.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a video call with Mr. Khoirul. He is your classmate. You both went to an animal park last Saturday. Talk about what you did there using Past Simple regular verbs.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hey! It's Khoirul! Last Saturday was so fun at the animal park, right? What was your favourite part? What animals did you like the most?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your classmate Mr. Khoirul visited an animal park last Saturday. Now you are talking about the trip. Share what you did, what animals you watched, and what you enjoyed.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student who went to an animal park with your classmate last Saturday. You are excited to talk about the trip and share your favourite moments.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I really enjoyed the animal park! I watched the elephants and I loved them. We walked around the park for two hours. I also photographed the birds. It was amazing!
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈrɪə.li ɪnˈdʒɔɪd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məl pɑːrk aɪ wɒtʃt ðə ˈɛl.ɪ.fənts ənd aɪ lʌvd ðɛm wiː wɔːkt əˈraʊnd ðə pɑːrk fɔːr tuː ˈaʊərz aɪ ˈɔːl.səʊ ˈfəʊ.tə.ɡrɑːft ðə bɜːdz ɪt wɒz əˈmeɪ.zɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Enjoyed' ends in /d/. 'Watched' ends in /t/. 'Walked' ends in /t/. 'Loved' ends in /d/. Notice the pattern: voiced sound before = /d/, voiceless sound before = /t/.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises sharing past experiences with a friend. You use multiple Past Simple verbs naturally in a casual, enthusiastic conversation about animals.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word clearly. These are regular verbs in Past Simple that we use to talk about animals and daily activities. Pay attention to the '-ed' ending.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say these past tense verbs one by one. Think about animals and what we do with them. Ready? Say each word after me.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: walked, played, cleaned, visited, watched, helped, arrived, liked, needed, enjoyed
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɔːkt/, /pleɪd/, /kliːnd/, /ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd/, /wɒtʃt/, /hɛlpt/, /əˈraɪvd/, /laɪkt/, /ˈniː.dɪd/, /ɪnˈdʒɔɪd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Group them by sound: /t/ ending = walked, watched, helped, liked. /d/ ending = played, cleaned, arrived, enjoyed. /ɪd/ ending = visited, needed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: These ten regular past tense verbs are essential for talking about animals and daily routines. Knowing how to pronounce each '-ed' ending correctly makes your English much clearer and more natural.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change each present tense sentence to Past Simple. Say the full sentence aloud with the correct past tense form.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: I will say a sentence in present tense. Please change it to past tense and say the full sentence. For example: 'I walk to school' becomes 'I walked to school.' Ready? Let's begin.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I walked to school yesterday. She cleaned the fish tank last night. We visited the zoo last weekend. They played with the dog after lunch. He watched the birds in the morning.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɔːkt tə skuːl ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə fɪʃ tæŋk lɑːst naɪt/ /wiː ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ðə zuː lɑːst ˌwiːkˈɛnd/ /ðeɪ pleɪd wɪð ðə dɒɡ ˈɑːf.tər lʌntʃ/ /hiː wɒtʃt ðə bɜːdz ɪn ðə ˈmɔːr.nɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Add '-ed' to the base verb. Remember to add a time word like 'yesterday', 'last night', or 'last weekend' to show it is in the past.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises forming Past Simple sentences with regular verbs. The key grammar rule is: Subject + verb-ed + rest of sentence + past time expression. No auxiliary 'did' is needed in positive statements.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word and pay attention to which syllable is stressed. The stressed syllable is shown in CAPITAL letters. Tap your hand on the stressed part.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern of each word. The stressed syllable is louder and longer. Repeat after me and make sure you stress the correct syllable.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: VIS-it-ed, ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, NEED-ed, re-FUSED, NO-ticed, OF-fered, WANT-ed, col-LECT-ed, pre-FERRED
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd/, /əˈraɪvd/, /ɪnˈdʒɔɪd/, /ˈniː.dɪd/, /rɪˈfjuːzd/, /ˈnəʊ.tɪst/, /ˈɒf.əd/, /ˈwɒn.tɪd/, /kəˈlɛk.tɪd/, /prɪˈfɜːd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Two-syllable verbs that end in '-ed' with /ɪd/ keep their original stress: VIS-it-ed, WANT-ed, NEED-ed. Verbs with stress on the second syllable keep it there: ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, re-FUSED, pre-FERRED, col-LECT-ed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Syllable stress does not change when you add '-ed' to a regular verb. The stress stays on the same syllable as the base form. However, verbs ending in /t/ or /d/ gain an extra syllable, which can change the rhythm. Practise tapping the stressed syllable to feel the pattern.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise rising and falling intonation. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for yes/no questions. Use FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for statements and wh-questions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the difference between questions and statements. When I ask 'Did you walk the dog?', my voice goes UP at the end. When I say 'I walked the dog', my voice goes DOWN. Now you try these sentences.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Did you walk the dog yesterday? ↗ I walked the dog yesterday. ↘ Did she clean the cage? ↗ She cleaned the cage. ↘ What time did you arrive? ↘ Did they enjoy the trip? ↗
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /dɪd juː wɔːk ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↗/ /aɪ wɔːkt ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↘/ /dɪd ʃiː kliːn ðə keɪdʒ ↗/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə keɪdʒ ↘/ /wɒt taɪm dɪd juː əˈraɪv ↘/ /dɪd ðeɪ ɪnˈdʒɔɪ ðə trɪp ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: Yes/no questions ('Did you…?', 'Did she…?', 'Did they…?') always end with RISING intonation ↗. Statements ('I walked…', 'She cleaned…') and wh-questions ('What time did you…?') end with FALLING intonation ↘.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation is the music of English. Rising intonation at the end of a yes/no question signals that you expect an answer. Falling intonation at the end of a statement shows you are giving information. In Past Simple, 'Did you…?' questions use rising intonation, while answers like 'Yes, I walked the dog' use falling intonation. Wh-questions like 'What did you do?' also use falling intonation because they ask for specific information, not just yes or no.

content.summary: Ujian akhir unit resmi untuk Unit 11: Animal World: Past Simple Regular Verbs. Menguji 4 kompetensi terintegrasi (Reading 15 soal, Listening 15 soal, Writing 10 soal, Speaking 15 soal) untuk menghasilkan scorecard nilai resmi per unit.

reading.question: According to the passage, when did Maria and Leo visit the animal shelter?
reading.explanation: The very first sentence says: 'Last Saturday, Maria and Leo visited an animal shelter near their house.' The time expression 'Last Saturday' tells us exactly when the visit happened.

reading.question: Which sentence uses the correct Past Simple negative form?
options: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
Maria didn't cleaned the dog cages.
Maria not cleaned the dog cages.
reading.answer: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
reading.explanation: In Past Simple negative sentences, we use 'didn't' + base verb (without -ed). 'Didn't clean' is correct. 'Didn't cleaned' is wrong because we don't add -ed after 'didn't.'

reading.question: In the passage, what did the green parrot do?
options: It talked and repeated funny words.
It jumped out of the cage.
reading.answer: It talked and repeated funny words.
reading.explanation: The passage says: 'A green parrot talked and repeated funny words.' Both 'talked' and 'repeated' are Past Simple regular verbs ending in -ed.

reading.question: What is the correct Past Simple form of the verb 'carry'?
reading.explanation: When a verb ends in consonant + y (like 'carry'), we change the y to i and add -ed. So 'carry' becomes 'carried.' This spelling rule is important to remember!

reading.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'They walked home with Snowball in a special box.' What does 'walked' tell us?
options: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
reading.answer: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
reading.explanation: The verb 'walked' ends in -ed, which means it is in the Past Simple tense. This tells us the action already happened and is complete. The whole story is about events that happened last Saturday.

reading.question: Which is the correct Past Simple question form?
reading.explanation: In Past Simple questions, we use 'Did' + subject + base verb (without -ed). 'Did they help' is correct. We don't add -ed to the verb after 'Did' because 'Did' already shows the past tense.

reading.question: What name did Maria and Leo give to their new cat?
reading.explanation: The passage says: 'They named her Snowball.' The verb 'named' is also a Past Simple regular verb (name → named: just add -d because the base verb already ends in -e).

reading.question: Look at these two sentences: 'Leo walked two big dogs.' and 'Leo didn't walk the cats.' Why does the second sentence use 'walk' instead of 'walked'?
options: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
Because negative sentences are always in the present tense.
reading.answer: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
reading.explanation: This is a very important rule! In negative Past Simple sentences, 'didn't' carries the past meaning. The main verb returns to its base form (walk, not walked). This is a common mistake for beginners, so remember: didn't + base verb.

reading.question: What time does the train to London depart?
reading.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

reading.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday, we _____ a new car.'
reading.explanation: 'Buy' is an irregular verb whose past simple form is 'bought'.

reading.question: What does Maria do every Saturday morning?
reading.explanation: A routine action in the simple present tense describing Saturday morning.

reading.question: Which question is grammatically correct?
reading.explanation: Standard question order: Question Word + Auxiliary (do) + Subject (you) + Verb (live).

reading.question: What is the opposite of 'expensive'?
reading.explanation: 'Cheap' means low in price, which is the direct opposite of 'expensive'.

reading.question: Choose the correct preposition: 'The keys are _____ the table.'
reading.explanation: We use 'on' when an object is physically resting on a surface.

reading.question: Which sentence expresses a future plan?
options: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
I visit my grandmother every day.
reading.answer: I am going to visit my grandmother tomorrow.
reading.explanation: 'Be going to' expresses a planned future intention.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about an animal you liked when you were young. Use Past Simple regular verbs. Follow the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds.
speaking.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me a story about an animal you liked when you were a child. What animal was it? What did you do with it? What happened one special day?
storyPoints: Name the animal and describe what it looked like (e.g., 'I liked a small brown cat.')
Tell what you usually did with the animal (e.g., 'I played with it every day. I cleaned its bowl.')
Describe one special thing that happened (e.g., 'One day, it jumped on my bed and I laughed.')
speaking.targetSentence: When I was young, I liked a small cat. I played with it every day and I cleaned its bowl. One day, it jumped on my bed and I laughed.
speaking.phonetic: /wɛn aɪ wɒz jʌŋ aɪ laɪkt ə smɔːl kæt aɪ pleɪd wɪð ɪt ˈɛv.ri deɪ ənd aɪ kliːnd ɪts bəʊl wʌn deɪ ɪt dʒʌmpt ɒn maɪ bɛd ənd aɪ lɑːft/
speaking.hint: Remember: 'liked' ends in /t/, 'played' ends in /d/, 'cleaned' ends in /d/, 'jumped' ends in /t/. Keep your story simple and use past tense.
speaking.explanation: This task practises storytelling fluency using Past Simple regular verbs. You need to connect ideas in order: introduce the animal, describe regular activities, and tell about a special event. Focus on correct '-ed' pronunciation.

speaking.instruction: Tell a short story about a visit to a zoo or a farm. Use Past Simple regular verbs. Follow the three story points below. Speak for about 30 seconds.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please tell me about a time you visited a zoo or a farm. Where did you go? What animals did you see? What did you enjoy the most?
storyPoints: Say where you went and when (e.g., 'Last year, I visited a zoo with my family.')
Describe the animals you watched or liked (e.g., 'I watched the monkeys. They climbed the trees.')
Tell what you enjoyed the most (e.g., 'I really enjoyed the bird show. The birds danced and we clapped.')
speaking.targetSentence: Last year, I visited a zoo with my family. I watched the monkeys and they climbed the trees. I really enjoyed the bird show. We clapped and laughed.
speaking.phonetic: /lɑːst jɪər aɪ ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ə zuː wɪð maɪ ˈfæm.ɪ.li aɪ wɒtʃt ðə ˈmʌŋ.kiz ənd ðeɪ klaɪmd ðə triːz aɪ ˈrɪə.li ɪnˈdʒɔɪd ðə bɜːd ʃəʊ wiː klæpt ənd lɑːft/
speaking.hint: 'Visited' has three syllables: VIS-it-ed (/ɪd/ ending). 'Watched' has one syllable: /wɒtʃt/ (/t/ ending). 'Enjoyed' has two syllables: en-JOYED (/d/ ending).
speaking.explanation: This storytelling task builds your ability to narrate a past experience in sequence. You practise mixing different '-ed' pronunciations in a natural story about animals.

speaking.instruction: You will have a phone call with Mr. Khoirul. He is a zookeeper. He will ask you about your pet. Answer his questions using Past Simple regular verbs. Be ready to ask him one question too.

speaking.phonetic: /ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ aɪ wɔːkt maɪ dɒɡ ɪn ðə pɑːrk aɪ kliːnd hɪz bəʊl ənd aɪ pleɪd wɪð hɪm dɪd juː fiːd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məlz ət ðə zuː təˈdeɪ/

speaking.phonetic: /jɛs aɪ ˈnəʊ.tɪst ə smɔːl kæt nɪər maɪ ˈɡɑːr.dən ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ɪt lʊkt skɛəd aɪ traɪd tə kɔːl ɪt bʌt ɪt wɔːkt əˈweɪ aɪ sɜːtʃt əˈraʊnd ðə ˈɡɑːr.dən bʌt aɪ ˈdɪd.ənt faɪnd ɪt/

speaking.audioPrompt: Good morning! This is Dr. Khoirul at the animal clinic. How can I help you today? You said your rabbit was not feeling well yesterday. Can you tell me what happened?
speaking.scenarioContext: You are calling the animal clinic because your pet rabbit was sick yesterday. Dr. Khoirul, the veterinarian, needs to know what symptoms you noticed and what you did to help your rabbit.
speaking.characterRole: You are a pet owner who is worried about your rabbit. Yesterday your rabbit looked tired and didn't eat. Tell the doctor what you noticed and what you did.
speaking.targetSentence: Yesterday, my rabbit looked very tired. It didn't move much. I offered it some food but it refused to eat. I cleaned its cage and I placed fresh water inside.
speaking.phonetic: /ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ maɪ ˈræb.ɪt lʊkt ˈvɛr.i ˈtaɪəd ɪt ˈdɪd.ənt muːv mʌtʃ aɪ ˈɒf.əd ɪt sʌm fuːd bʌt ɪt rɪˈfjuːzd tə iːt aɪ kliːnd ɪts keɪdʒ ənd aɪ pleɪst frɛʃ ˈwɔː.tər ɪnˈsaɪd/

speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises describing a problem in the past. You use Past Simple to explain symptoms and actions, which is a practical life skill when visiting an animal doctor.

speaking.audioPrompt: Hey! It's Khoirul! Last Saturday was so fun at the animal park, right? What was your favourite part? What animals did you like the most?
speaking.scenarioContext: You and your classmate Mr. Khoirul visited an animal park last Saturday. Now you are talking about the trip. Share what you did, what animals you watched, and what you enjoyed.

speaking.phonetic: /aɪ ˈrɪə.li ɪnˈdʒɔɪd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məl pɑːrk aɪ wɒtʃt ðə ˈɛl.ɪ.fənts ənd aɪ lʌvd ðɛm wiː wɔːkt əˈraʊnd ðə pɑːrk fɔːr tuː ˈaʊərz aɪ ˈɔːl.səʊ ˈfəʊ.tə.ɡrɑːft ðə bɜːdz ɪt wɒz əˈmeɪ.zɪŋ/
speaking.hint: 'Enjoyed' ends in /d/. 'Watched' ends in /t/. 'Walked' ends in /t/. 'Loved' ends in /d/. Notice the pattern: voiced sound before = /d/, voiceless sound before = /t/.
speaking.explanation: This roleplay practises sharing past experiences with a friend. You use multiple Past Simple verbs naturally in a casual, enthusiastic conversation about animals.

speaking.instruction: Say each word clearly. These are regular verbs in Past Simple that we use to talk about animals and daily activities. Pay attention to the '-ed' ending.
speaking.audioPrompt: Please say these past tense verbs one by one. Think about animals and what we do with them. Ready? Say each word after me.
speaking.targetSentence: walked, played, cleaned, visited, watched, helped, arrived, liked, needed, enjoyed
speaking.hint: Group them by sound: /t/ ending = walked, watched, helped, liked. /d/ ending = played, cleaned, arrived, enjoyed. /ɪd/ ending = visited, needed.
speaking.explanation: These ten regular past tense verbs are essential for talking about animals and daily routines. Knowing how to pronounce each '-ed' ending correctly makes your English much clearer and more natural.

speaking.instruction: Change each present tense sentence to Past Simple. Say the full sentence aloud with the correct past tense form.
speaking.audioPrompt: I will say a sentence in present tense. Please change it to past tense and say the full sentence. For example: 'I walk to school' becomes 'I walked to school.' Ready? Let's begin.
speaking.targetSentence: I walked to school yesterday. She cleaned the fish tank last night. We visited the zoo last weekend. They played with the dog after lunch. He watched the birds in the morning.
speaking.phonetic: /aɪ wɔːkt tə skuːl ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə fɪʃ tæŋk lɑːst naɪt/ /wiː ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ðə zuː lɑːst ˌwiːkˈɛnd/ /ðeɪ pleɪd wɪð ðə dɒɡ ˈɑːf.tər lʌntʃ/ /hiː wɒtʃt ðə bɜːdz ɪn ðə ˈmɔːr.nɪŋ/
speaking.hint: Add '-ed' to the base verb. Remember to add a time word like 'yesterday', 'last night', or 'last weekend' to show it is in the past.
speaking.explanation: This drill practises forming Past Simple sentences with regular verbs. The key grammar rule is: Subject + verb-ed + rest of sentence + past time expression. No auxiliary 'did' is needed in positive statements.

speaking.instruction: Say each word and pay attention to which syllable is stressed. The stressed syllable is shown in CAPITAL letters. Tap your hand on the stressed part.
speaking.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern of each word. The stressed syllable is louder and longer. Repeat after me and make sure you stress the correct syllable.
speaking.targetSentence: VIS-it-ed, ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, NEED-ed, re-FUSED, NO-ticed, OF-fered, WANT-ed, col-LECT-ed, pre-FERRED
speaking.hint: Two-syllable verbs that end in '-ed' with /ɪd/ keep their original stress: VIS-it-ed, WANT-ed, NEED-ed. Verbs with stress on the second syllable keep it there: ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, re-FUSED, pre-FERRED, col-LECT-ed.
speaking.explanation: Syllable stress does not change when you add '-ed' to a regular verb. The stress stays on the same syllable as the base form. However, verbs ending in /t/ or /d/ gain an extra syllable, which can change the rhythm. Practise tapping the stressed syllable to feel the pattern.

speaking.instruction: Practise rising and falling intonation. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for yes/no questions. Use FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for statements and wh-questions.
speaking.audioPrompt: Listen to the difference between questions and statements. When I ask 'Did you walk the dog?', my voice goes UP at the end. When I say 'I walked the dog', my voice goes DOWN. Now you try these sentences.
speaking.targetSentence: Did you walk the dog yesterday? ↗ I walked the dog yesterday. ↘ Did she clean the cage? ↗ She cleaned the cage. ↘ What time did you arrive? ↘ Did they enjoy the trip? ↗
speaking.phonetic: /dɪd juː wɔːk ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↗/ /aɪ wɔːkt ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↘/ /dɪd ʃiː kliːn ðə keɪdʒ ↗/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə keɪdʒ ↘/ /wɒt taɪm dɪd juː əˈraɪv ↘/ /dɪd ðeɪ ɪnˈdʒɔɪ ðə trɪp ↗/
speaking.hint: Yes/no questions ('Did you…?', 'Did she…?', 'Did they…?') always end with RISING intonation ↗. Statements ('I walked…', 'She cleaned…') and wh-questions ('What time did you…?') end with FALLING intonation ↘.
speaking.explanation: Intonation is the music of English. Rising intonation at the end of a yes/no question signals that you expect an answer. Falling intonation at the end of a statement shows you are giving information. In Past Simple, 'Did you…?' questions use rising intonation, while answers like 'Yes, I walked the dog' use falling intonation. Wh-questions like 'What did you do?' also use falling intonation because they ask for specific information, not just yes or no.

questions.question: According to the passage, when did Maria and Leo visit the animal shelter?
questions.explanation: The very first sentence says: 'Last Saturday, Maria and Leo visited an animal shelter near their house.' The time expression 'Last Saturday' tells us exactly when the visit happened.

questions.question: Which sentence uses the correct Past Simple negative form?
options: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
Maria didn't cleaned the dog cages.
Maria not cleaned the dog cages.
questions.answer: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
questions.explanation: In Past Simple negative sentences, we use 'didn't' + base verb (without -ed). 'Didn't clean' is correct. 'Didn't cleaned' is wrong because we don't add -ed after 'didn't.'

questions.question: In the passage, what did the green parrot do?
options: It talked and repeated funny words.
It jumped out of the cage.
questions.answer: It talked and repeated funny words.
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'A green parrot talked and repeated funny words.' Both 'talked' and 'repeated' are Past Simple regular verbs ending in -ed.

questions.question: What is the correct Past Simple form of the verb 'carry'?
questions.explanation: When a verb ends in consonant + y (like 'carry'), we change the y to i and add -ed. So 'carry' becomes 'carried.' This spelling rule is important to remember!

questions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'They walked home with Snowball in a special box.' What does 'walked' tell us?
options: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
questions.answer: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
questions.explanation: The verb 'walked' ends in -ed, which means it is in the Past Simple tense. This tells us the action already happened and is complete. The whole story is about events that happened last Saturday.

questions.question: Which is the correct Past Simple question form?
questions.explanation: In Past Simple questions, we use 'Did' + subject + base verb (without -ed). 'Did they help' is correct. We don't add -ed to the verb after 'Did' because 'Did' already shows the past tense.

questions.question: What name did Maria and Leo give to their new cat?
questions.explanation: The passage says: 'They named her Snowball.' The verb 'named' is also a Past Simple regular verb (name → named: just add -d because the base verb already ends in -e).

questions.question: Look at these two sentences: 'Leo walked two big dogs.' and 'Leo didn't walk the cats.' Why does the second sentence use 'walk' instead of 'walked'?
options: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
Because negative sentences are always in the present tense.
questions.answer: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
questions.explanation: This is a very important rule! In negative Past Simple sentences, 'didn't' carries the past meaning. The main verb returns to its base form (walk, not walked). This is a common mistake for beginners, so remember: didn't + base verb.

questions.question: What time does the train to London depart?
questions.explanation: Standard timetable questions provide specific morning departure times.

questions.question: Choose the correct past form: 'Yesterday, we _____ a new car.'

questions.question: What does Maria do every Saturday morning?

questions.question: Which question is grammatically correct?
questions.explanation: Standard question order: Question Word + Auxiliary (do) + Subject (you) + Verb (live).

questions.question: What is the opposite of 'expensive'?
questions.explanation: 'Cheap' means low in price, which is the direct opposite of 'expensive'.

questions.question: Choose the correct preposition: 'The keys are _____ the table.'
questions.explanation: We use 'on' when an object is physically resting on a surface.

questions.question: Which sentence expresses a future plan?

questions.explanation: 'Be going to' expresses a planned future intention.

questions.phonetic: /aɪ wɔːkt tə skuːl ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə fɪʃ tæŋk lɑːst naɪt/ /wiː ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ðə zuː lɑːst ˌwiːkˈɛnd/ /ðeɪ pleɪd wɪð ðə dɒɡ ˈɑːf.tər lʌntʃ/ /hiː wɒtʃt ðə bɜːdz ɪn ðə ˈmɔːr.nɪŋ/

questions.instruction: Say each word and pay attention to which syllable is stressed. The stressed syllable is shown in CAPITAL letters. Tap your hand on the stressed part.
questions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern of each word. The stressed syllable is louder and longer. Repeat after me and make sure you stress the correct syllable.
questions.targetSentence: VIS-it-ed, ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, NEED-ed, re-FUSED, NO-ticed, OF-fered, WANT-ed, col-LECT-ed, pre-FERRED
questions.hint: Two-syllable verbs that end in '-ed' with /ɪd/ keep their original stress: VIS-it-ed, WANT-ed, NEED-ed. Verbs with stress on the second syllable keep it there: ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, re-FUSED, pre-FERRED, col-LECT-ed.
questions.explanation: Syllable stress does not change when you add '-ed' to a regular verb. The stress stays on the same syllable as the base form. However, verbs ending in /t/ or /d/ gain an extra syllable, which can change the rhythm. Practise tapping the stressed syllable to feel the pattern.

questions.instruction: Practise rising and falling intonation. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for yes/no questions. Use FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for statements and wh-questions.
questions.audioPrompt: Listen to the difference between questions and statements. When I ask 'Did you walk the dog?', my voice goes UP at the end. When I say 'I walked the dog', my voice goes DOWN. Now you try these sentences.
questions.targetSentence: Did you walk the dog yesterday? ↗ I walked the dog yesterday. ↘ Did she clean the cage? ↗ She cleaned the cage. ↘ What time did you arrive? ↘ Did they enjoy the trip? ↗
questions.phonetic: /dɪd juː wɔːk ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↗/ /aɪ wɔːkt ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↘/ /dɪd ʃiː kliːn ðə keɪdʒ ↗/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə keɪdʒ ↘/ /wɒt taɪm dɪd juː əˈraɪv ↘/ /dɪd ðeɪ ɪnˈdʒɔɪ ðə trɪp ↗/
questions.hint: Yes/no questions ('Did you…?', 'Did she…?', 'Did they…?') always end with RISING intonation ↗. Statements ('I walked…', 'She cleaned…') and wh-questions ('What time did you…?') end with FALLING intonation ↘.
questions.explanation: Intonation is the music of English. Rising intonation at the end of a yes/no question signals that you expect an answer. Falling intonation at the end of a statement shows you are giving information. In Past Simple, 'Did you…?' questions use rising intonation, while answers like 'Yes, I walked the dog' use falling intonation. Wh-questions like 'What did you do?' also use falling intonation because they ask for specific information, not just yes or no.

practicumQuestions.question: Which sentence uses the correct Past Simple negative form?
options: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
Maria didn't cleaned the dog cages.
Maria not cleaned the dog cages.
practicumQuestions.answer: Maria didn't clean the dog cages.
practicumQuestions.explanation: In Past Simple negative sentences, we use 'didn't' + base verb (without -ed). 'Didn't clean' is correct. 'Didn't cleaned' is wrong because we don't add -ed after 'didn't.'

practicumQuestions.question: In the passage, what did the green parrot do?
options: It talked and repeated funny words.
It jumped out of the cage.
practicumQuestions.answer: It talked and repeated funny words.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'A green parrot talked and repeated funny words.' Both 'talked' and 'repeated' are Past Simple regular verbs ending in -ed.

practicumQuestions.question: What is the correct Past Simple form of the verb 'carry'?
practicumQuestions.explanation: When a verb ends in consonant + y (like 'carry'), we change the y to i and add -ed. So 'carry' becomes 'carried.' This spelling rule is important to remember!

practicumQuestions.question: Read this sentence from the passage: 'They walked home with Snowball in a special box.' What does 'walked' tell us?
options: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
practicumQuestions.answer: The action of walking happened in the past and is finished.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The verb 'walked' ends in -ed, which means it is in the Past Simple tense. This tells us the action already happened and is complete. The whole story is about events that happened last Saturday.

practicumQuestions.question: Which is the correct Past Simple question form?
practicumQuestions.explanation: In Past Simple questions, we use 'Did' + subject + base verb (without -ed). 'Did they help' is correct. We don't add -ed to the verb after 'Did' because 'Did' already shows the past tense.

practicumQuestions.question: What name did Maria and Leo give to their new cat?
practicumQuestions.explanation: The passage says: 'They named her Snowball.' The verb 'named' is also a Past Simple regular verb (name → named: just add -d because the base verb already ends in -e).

practicumQuestions.question: Look at these two sentences: 'Leo walked two big dogs.' and 'Leo didn't walk the cats.' Why does the second sentence use 'walk' instead of 'walked'?
options: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
Because negative sentences are always in the present tense.
practicumQuestions.answer: Because 'didn't' already shows the past tense, so the main verb stays in its base form.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This is a very important rule! In negative Past Simple sentences, 'didn't' carries the past meaning. The main verb returns to its base form (walk, not walked). This is a common mistake for beginners, so remember: didn't + base verb.

practicumQuestions.prompt: Write 3 sentences about what animals did at a farm yesterday. Use Past Simple regular verbs (positive and negative). Include a time word.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about an animal you liked when you were young. Use Past Simple regular verbs. Follow the three story points below to guide your story. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Now, please tell me a story about an animal you liked when you were a child. What animal was it? What did you do with it? What happened one special day?
storyPoints: Name the animal and describe what it looked like (e.g., 'I liked a small brown cat.')
Tell what you usually did with the animal (e.g., 'I played with it every day. I cleaned its bowl.')
Describe one special thing that happened (e.g., 'One day, it jumped on my bed and I laughed.')
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: When I was young, I liked a small cat. I played with it every day and I cleaned its bowl. One day, it jumped on my bed and I laughed.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɛn aɪ wɒz jʌŋ aɪ laɪkt ə smɔːl kæt aɪ pleɪd wɪð ɪt ˈɛv.ri deɪ ənd aɪ kliːnd ɪts bəʊl wʌn deɪ ɪt dʒʌmpt ɒn maɪ bɛd ənd aɪ lɑːft/
practicumQuestions.hint: Remember: 'liked' ends in /t/, 'played' ends in /d/, 'cleaned' ends in /d/, 'jumped' ends in /t/. Keep your story simple and use past tense.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This task practises storytelling fluency using Past Simple regular verbs. You need to connect ideas in order: introduce the animal, describe regular activities, and tell about a special event. Focus on correct '-ed' pronunciation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Tell a short story about a visit to a zoo or a farm. Use Past Simple regular verbs. Follow the three story points below. Speak for about 30 seconds.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please tell me about a time you visited a zoo or a farm. Where did you go? What animals did you see? What did you enjoy the most?
storyPoints: Say where you went and when (e.g., 'Last year, I visited a zoo with my family.')
Describe the animals you watched or liked (e.g., 'I watched the monkeys. They climbed the trees.')
Tell what you enjoyed the most (e.g., 'I really enjoyed the bird show. The birds danced and we clapped.')
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Last year, I visited a zoo with my family. I watched the monkeys and they climbed the trees. I really enjoyed the bird show. We clapped and laughed.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /lɑːst jɪər aɪ ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ə zuː wɪð maɪ ˈfæm.ɪ.li aɪ wɒtʃt ðə ˈmʌŋ.kiz ənd ðeɪ klaɪmd ðə triːz aɪ ˈrɪə.li ɪnˈdʒɔɪd ðə bɜːd ʃəʊ wiː klæpt ənd lɑːft/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Visited' has three syllables: VIS-it-ed (/ɪd/ ending). 'Watched' has one syllable: /wɒtʃt/ (/t/ ending). 'Enjoyed' has two syllables: en-JOYED (/d/ ending).
practicumQuestions.explanation: This storytelling task builds your ability to narrate a past experience in sequence. You practise mixing different '-ed' pronunciations in a natural story about animals.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a phone call with Mr. Khoirul. He is a zookeeper. He will ask you about your pet. Answer his questions using Past Simple regular verbs. Be ready to ask him one question too.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Ring ring! Hello, this is Mr. Khoirul from the city zoo. I heard you have a pet at home. Can you tell me about your pet? What did you do with your pet yesterday?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling the city zoo to ask about animal care. The zookeeper, Mr. Khoirul, is friendly and wants to know about your pet too. You talk about what you did with your pet yesterday and ask him about the zoo animals.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student who has a pet at home. You called the zoo because you want to learn how to take care of your pet better. Tell Mr. Khoirul what you did with your pet yesterday.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yesterday, I walked my dog in the park. I cleaned his bowl and I played with him. Did you feed the animals at the zoo today?
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ aɪ wɔːkt maɪ dɒɡ ɪn ðə pɑːrk aɪ kliːnd hɪz bəʊl ənd aɪ pleɪd wɪð hɪm dɪd juː fiːd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məlz ət ðə zuː təˈdeɪ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Use past tense for yesterday's actions: 'walked', 'cleaned', 'played'. Ask a question with 'Did you…?' and let your voice rise at the end.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises real conversation skills. You answer questions about past activities and also ask a question, showing you can use Past Simple in both statements and questions.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a video call with Mr. Khoirul. He is your neighbour. His cat is missing. He asks you if you noticed anything yesterday. Answer using Past Simple regular verbs.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hello! This is Mr. Khoirul, your neighbour. My cat Milo is missing! I'm very worried. Did you see anything unusual yesterday near your house?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: Your neighbour Mr. Khoirul has lost his cat named Milo. He calls you to ask if you noticed anything yesterday. You try to help by telling him what you observed near your house yesterday.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a helpful neighbour. Yesterday you noticed a small cat near your garden. Tell Mr. Khoirul what you saw and what happened.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yes, I noticed a small cat near my garden yesterday. It looked scared. I tried to call it but it walked away. I searched around the garden but I didn't find it.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /jɛs aɪ ˈnəʊ.tɪst ə smɔːl kæt nɪər maɪ ˈɡɑːr.dən ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ɪt lʊkt skɛəd aɪ traɪd tə kɔːl ɪt bʌt ɪt wɔːkt əˈweɪ aɪ sɜːtʃt əˈraʊnd ðə ˈɡɑːr.dən bʌt aɪ ˈdɪd.ənt faɪnd ɪt/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Noticed' = NO-ticed (two syllables, /t/ ending). 'Looked' = one syllable (/t/ ending). 'Tried' = one syllable (/d/ ending). 'Searched' = one syllable (/t/ ending).
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay builds your ability to describe past observations. You practise multiple regular past tense verbs in a realistic, helpful conversation about a missing pet.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a phone call with Mr. Khoirul. He is a veterinarian (animal doctor). You are calling because your rabbit was sick yesterday. Tell him what happened using Past Simple regular verbs.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Good morning! This is Dr. Khoirul at the animal clinic. How can I help you today? You said your rabbit was not feeling well yesterday. Can you tell me what happened?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You are calling the animal clinic because your pet rabbit was sick yesterday. Dr. Khoirul, the veterinarian, needs to know what symptoms you noticed and what you did to help your rabbit.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a pet owner who is worried about your rabbit. Yesterday your rabbit looked tired and didn't eat. Tell the doctor what you noticed and what you did.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Yesterday, my rabbit looked very tired. It didn't move much. I offered it some food but it refused to eat. I cleaned its cage and I placed fresh water inside.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ maɪ ˈræb.ɪt lʊkt ˈvɛr.i ˈtaɪəd ɪt ˈdɪd.ənt muːv mʌtʃ aɪ ˈɒf.əd ɪt sʌm fuːd bʌt ɪt rɪˈfjuːzd tə iːt aɪ kliːnd ɪts keɪdʒ ənd aɪ pleɪst frɛʃ ˈwɔː.tər ɪnˈsaɪd/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Offered' = OF-fered (two syllables, /d/ ending). 'Refused' = re-FUSED (two syllables, /d/ ending). 'Placed' = one syllable (/t/ ending).
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises describing a problem in the past. You use Past Simple to explain symptoms and actions, which is a practical life skill when visiting an animal doctor.

practicumQuestions.instruction: You will have a video call with Mr. Khoirul. He is your classmate. You both went to an animal park last Saturday. Talk about what you did there using Past Simple regular verbs.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Hey! It's Khoirul! Last Saturday was so fun at the animal park, right? What was your favourite part? What animals did you like the most?
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: You and your classmate Mr. Khoirul visited an animal park last Saturday. Now you are talking about the trip. Share what you did, what animals you watched, and what you enjoyed.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a student who went to an animal park with your classmate last Saturday. You are excited to talk about the trip and share your favourite moments.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I really enjoyed the animal park! I watched the elephants and I loved them. We walked around the park for two hours. I also photographed the birds. It was amazing!
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ ˈrɪə.li ɪnˈdʒɔɪd ðə ˈæn.ɪ.məl pɑːrk aɪ wɒtʃt ðə ˈɛl.ɪ.fənts ənd aɪ lʌvd ðɛm wiː wɔːkt əˈraʊnd ðə pɑːrk fɔːr tuː ˈaʊərz aɪ ˈɔːl.səʊ ˈfəʊ.tə.ɡrɑːft ðə bɜːdz ɪt wɒz əˈmeɪ.zɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: 'Enjoyed' ends in /d/. 'Watched' ends in /t/. 'Walked' ends in /t/. 'Loved' ends in /d/. Notice the pattern: voiced sound before = /d/, voiceless sound before = /t/.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This roleplay practises sharing past experiences with a friend. You use multiple Past Simple verbs naturally in a casual, enthusiastic conversation about animals.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word clearly. These are regular verbs in Past Simple that we use to talk about animals and daily activities. Pay attention to the '-ed' ending.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Please say these past tense verbs one by one. Think about animals and what we do with them. Ready? Say each word after me.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: walked, played, cleaned, visited, watched, helped, arrived, liked, needed, enjoyed
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wɔːkt/, /pleɪd/, /kliːnd/, /ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd/, /wɒtʃt/, /hɛlpt/, /əˈraɪvd/, /laɪkt/, /ˈniː.dɪd/, /ɪnˈdʒɔɪd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Group them by sound: /t/ ending = walked, watched, helped, liked. /d/ ending = played, cleaned, arrived, enjoyed. /ɪd/ ending = visited, needed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: These ten regular past tense verbs are essential for talking about animals and daily routines. Knowing how to pronounce each '-ed' ending correctly makes your English much clearer and more natural.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change each present tense sentence to Past Simple. Say the full sentence aloud with the correct past tense form.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: I will say a sentence in present tense. Please change it to past tense and say the full sentence. For example: 'I walk to school' becomes 'I walked to school.' Ready? Let's begin.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I walked to school yesterday. She cleaned the fish tank last night. We visited the zoo last weekend. They played with the dog after lunch. He watched the birds in the morning.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wɔːkt tə skuːl ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə fɪʃ tæŋk lɑːst naɪt/ /wiː ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd ðə zuː lɑːst ˌwiːkˈɛnd/ /ðeɪ pleɪd wɪð ðə dɒɡ ˈɑːf.tər lʌntʃ/ /hiː wɒtʃt ðə bɜːdz ɪn ðə ˈmɔːr.nɪŋ/
practicumQuestions.hint: Add '-ed' to the base verb. Remember to add a time word like 'yesterday', 'last night', or 'last weekend' to show it is in the past.
practicumQuestions.explanation: This drill practises forming Past Simple sentences with regular verbs. The key grammar rule is: Subject + verb-ed + rest of sentence + past time expression. No auxiliary 'did' is needed in positive statements.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word and pay attention to which syllable is stressed. The stressed syllable is shown in CAPITAL letters. Tap your hand on the stressed part.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the stress pattern of each word. The stressed syllable is louder and longer. Repeat after me and make sure you stress the correct syllable.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: VIS-it-ed, ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, NEED-ed, re-FUSED, NO-ticed, OF-fered, WANT-ed, col-LECT-ed, pre-FERRED
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /ˈvɪz.ɪ.tɪd/, /əˈraɪvd/, /ɪnˈdʒɔɪd/, /ˈniː.dɪd/, /rɪˈfjuːzd/, /ˈnəʊ.tɪst/, /ˈɒf.əd/, /ˈwɒn.tɪd/, /kəˈlɛk.tɪd/, /prɪˈfɜːd/
practicumQuestions.hint: Two-syllable verbs that end in '-ed' with /ɪd/ keep their original stress: VIS-it-ed, WANT-ed, NEED-ed. Verbs with stress on the second syllable keep it there: ar-RIVED, en-JOYED, re-FUSED, pre-FERRED, col-LECT-ed.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Syllable stress does not change when you add '-ed' to a regular verb. The stress stays on the same syllable as the base form. However, verbs ending in /t/ or /d/ gain an extra syllable, which can change the rhythm. Practise tapping the stressed syllable to feel the pattern.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Practise rising and falling intonation. Use RISING intonation (voice goes up) for yes/no questions. Use FALLING intonation (voice goes down) for statements and wh-questions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Listen to the difference between questions and statements. When I ask 'Did you walk the dog?', my voice goes UP at the end. When I say 'I walked the dog', my voice goes DOWN. Now you try these sentences.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Did you walk the dog yesterday? ↗ I walked the dog yesterday. ↘ Did she clean the cage? ↗ She cleaned the cage. ↘ What time did you arrive? ↘ Did they enjoy the trip? ↗
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /dɪd juː wɔːk ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↗/ /aɪ wɔːkt ðə dɒɡ ˈjɛs.tə.deɪ ↘/ /dɪd ʃiː kliːn ðə keɪdʒ ↗/ /ʃiː kliːnd ðə keɪdʒ ↘/ /wɒt taɪm dɪd juː əˈraɪv ↘/ /dɪd ðeɪ ɪnˈdʒɔɪ ðə trɪp ↗/
practicumQuestions.hint: Yes/no questions ('Did you…?', 'Did she…?', 'Did they…?') always end with RISING intonation ↗. Statements ('I walked…', 'She cleaned…') and wh-questions ('What time did you…?') end with FALLING intonation ↘.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Intonation is the music of English. Rising intonation at the end of a yes/no question signals that you expect an answer. Falling intonation at the end of a statement shows you are giving information. In Past Simple, 'Did you…?' questions use rising intonation, while answers like 'Yes, I walked the dog' use falling intonation. Wh-questions like 'What did you do?' also use falling intonation because they ask for specific information, not just yes or no.
